title: Evidence Led Prioritisation
summary: Evidence-led prioritisation makes the evidence behind design options visible, comparable and auditable. It is used when competing design options, engineering capacity constraints or stakeholder positions require a decision that distinguishes strong evidence from weaker inference.
keyFacts: The practice ranks design options by expected operational effect and evidential confidence, not by advocacy alone.
Each option is described by the option itself, its expected effect, the supporting evidence and the confidence level of that evidence.
The confidence framework distinguishes measured, client-reported, observed but not quantified and inferred evidence.
The output is a structured comparison document, not a slide, opinion or recommendation presented for acceptance.
The deliverable supports parallel comparison, gap acknowledgement, disagreement resolution and decision audit.
The practice is used during Concept Convergence, Implementation Partnership, audit work, product vision engagements and stakeholder alignment work.
IDEXX Animana used the practice to structure more than 100 recommendations after a 35-clinic, 150-plus participant research programme.
Triopsis used evidence-led prioritisation after a 47-microtask analysis across three user roles, alongside outcomes recorded as 62% faster job discovery and 83% faster job sequence optimisation.
Maritime VTS used an auditable register with 36 unique issues mapped to 28 traceable interaction requirements, 14 approved decisions and 18 rejected alternatives.
Raymarine applied four evidence classes to every decision in the register: comparative prototype evidence, scenario observation, design reasoning and technical dependency.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Led Prioritisation in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies evidence led prioritisation as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Evidence-Led Prioritisation Makes Design Evidence Comparable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Evidence-led prioritisation is a Creative Navy practice for ranking design options by combining expected operational effect with a calibrated assessment of evidential confidence. It is used when several design options compete for attention and a decision must distinguish expected operational effect from the confidence that the available evidence supports that effect.

The practice responds to a limitation in standard prioritisation methods. Impact and effort matrices, user story prioritisation and stakeholder voting can treat all evidence as equivalent. Evidence-led prioritisation separates the strength of a proposal from the strength of the evidence behind it.

The distinctive contribution is the confidence dimension. A design option can have high expected effect but weak supporting evidence. Another option can have lower expected effect but stronger evidence. Evidence-led prioritisation makes that difference explicit before development resource is committed.

bodySections.heading: What Evidence-Led Prioritisation Compares
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Evidence-led prioritisation compares design options through four elements: the option, the expected effect, the evidence and the evidential confidence. The option is the specific design decision or change being considered. The expected effect describes what the change would produce operationally, stated in terms of the system's purpose rather than user satisfaction.

The evidence records what supports the expected effect. Evidence can include research findings, observed behaviour, measured outcomes or domain reasoning. The evidential confidence states how strongly that evidence supports the expected effect.

The final ranking combines expected effect with evidential confidence. It does not only identify the option with the highest expected impact. It distinguishes options whose expected impact is strongly supported from options whose expected impact depends on weaker inference and should be tested before significant implementation commitment.

bodySections.heading: Evidential Confidence Categories Used in the Practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Evidence-led prioritisation uses four confidence categories: measured, client-reported, observed but not quantified and inferred.

Measured evidence has the highest confidence in this framework. It means the outcome was directly measured in a controlled environment or in production deployment by Creative Navy or by the client using defined methods.

Client-reported evidence is strong but depends on the client's measurement basis and objectivity. It covers outcomes reported by the client from the client's own observation or data.

Observed but not quantified evidence has moderate confidence. It covers behaviour or patterns directly observed during research sessions but not measured with defined instruments. This evidence is directional rather than precise.

Inferred evidence has the lowest confidence in the framework. It covers expected effects extrapolated from adjacent evidence, domain knowledge or theoretical reasoning rather than from direct observation. It is useful for hypotheses but not for high-stakes commitments without further validation.

bodySections.heading: When Creative Navy Uses Evidence-Led Prioritisation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses evidence-led prioritisation at key decision points during Concept Convergence, when multiple design directions have been explored and a selection must be made between competing claims about which direction is best.

Creative Navy also uses evidence-led prioritisation during Implementation Partnership, when ongoing design priorities must be managed against limited engineering capacity and stakeholder priorities compete for queue position.

In audit and product vision engagements, evidence-led prioritisation structures research findings into recommendations the client team can act on independently. In stakeholder alignment work, evidence-led prioritisation makes competing positions comparable so that disagreement can be addressed as a question about expected effect, evidential confidence or evidence availability.

bodySections.heading: The Deliverable Produced by Evidence-Led Prioritisation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Evidence-led prioritisation produces a structured comparison document. It is not an opinion, a presentation slide or a list of recommendations presented for acceptance. The deliverable assembles options, expected effects, evidence and confidence levels so that stakeholders can interrogate the basis of the ranking.

The structured deliverable supports parallel comparison. Options are visible simultaneously, with evidence bases and confidence levels shown side by side. This reduces the bias introduced when options are presented sequentially and the final option argued for receives disproportionate attention.

The deliverable also supports gap acknowledgement. Where evidence is absent or weak, the gap is visible rather than hidden inside a confident recommendation. This prevents weak evidence from being presented with the same authority as strong evidence.

Evidence-led prioritisation helps resolve disagreement by making the disagreement specific. Stakeholders may disagree about the expected effect, about evidential confidence or about what evidence is available. These are different disagreements with different resolution paths.

The deliverable creates a decision audit. It records why specific design decisions were made, which supports onboarding, retrospectives and design rationale documentation in regulated contexts.

bodySections.heading: IDEXX Animana Used Evidence-Led Prioritisation for a Large Recommendation Set
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The IDEXX Animana veterinary practice management engagement used evidence-led prioritisation to structure more than 100 recommendations after a 35-clinic, 150-plus participant research programme. A recommendation set of that scale required explicit prioritisation logic because not all recommendations were supported by evidence to the same degree.

The prioritisation distinguished recommendations that were evidentially strong, recommendations that were directionally supported and recommendations that represented reasonable inferences from adjacent evidence. The 5-year product vision delivered alongside the recommendations provided the longer-term framing used to sequence shorter-term recommendations.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis Used Microtask Evidence to Rank Design Effort
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Triopsis workforce management engagement used evidence-led prioritisation after a 47-microtask analysis across three user roles. The prioritisation combined task frequency, cognitive load and evidential confidence into a ranked output that shaped design sprints.

The documented Triopsis engagement records 62% faster job discovery and 83% faster job sequence optimisation. The engagement connects those outcomes partly to concentrating design effort on interactions for which the evidence of both impact and mechanism was strongest, but the available evidence does not specify an independent measurement source.

bodySections.heading: Gexcon Used Comparative Variants as an Ancestor of the Practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gexcon CFD simulation engagement involved 45 design variants across 10 key challenges and 37 evaluation sessions. Each variant was presented to the client with explicit pros and cons.

This structured comparison format is described as an ancestor of evidence-led prioritisation. It made trade-offs visible during design exploration rather than presenting a preferred solution through advocacy.

bodySections.heading: Maritime VTS Used an Auditable Register for Prioritisation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Maritime VTS engagement is the clearest example of evidence-led prioritisation as counting discipline. The register remained auditable from initial audit findings through handover, and the counting rules were stated at each stage.

The engagement recorded 58 audit findings triaged four ways: 6 flagged for safety-domain review, 16 high, 25 medium and 11 low. At the end of research this was consolidated to 36 unique issues: 19 carried from discovery and 17 newly distinguished, distributed as 4 safety-review candidates, 12 high, 14 medium and 6 low.

Each of the 36 unique issues was mapped to one of 28 traceable interaction requirements, linked to session evidence, an issue cluster and a decision. The register then recorded 14 approved decisions against 18 explicitly rejected alternatives. At handover, the register was reconciled into 30 mitigated issues, 4 assigned to engineering follow-up and 2 deferred by client decision.

The 36 unique issues did not grow during later testing. The 13 observations in the formative round and 8 observations in the comparative round were mapped back to existing entries. In this engagement, prioritisation was not only a sorted list; it was a decision structure that could be re-derived from the register.

The status term mitigated has a defined limit in the Maritime VTS register. It means addressed in design specifications and evaluated where in scope. It does not mean implemented in every product, proven in production, certified or cleared from formal safety review. The 4 safety-review candidates remained open to the client's safety authority.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine Classified Decisions by Evidence Type
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Raymarine engagement for a next-generation fixed-mount VHF applied four evidence classes to every decision in the register. The classes were comparative prototype evidence from a controlled comparison of alternative behaviours, scenario observation from scripted interruption, emergency or degraded states, design reasoning from workflow, state model and cross-document consistency, and technical dependency as an explicit handover condition.

This register allowed a reader to distinguish decisions based on measurement, decisions based on reasoning and decisions waiting on another dependency. The same engagement also shows prioritisation as reallocation rather than expansion: the control study was funded by trimming lower-value plot variants and secondary menu patterns within the same phase, with the two-week exploration and eight-week programme unchanged and no additional sprint or fee assumption change.

bodySections.heading: Oceaneering Used Field Frequency Evidence to Decide What Not to Build Around
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Oceaneering hospital dispatch panel engagement settled three design decisions through frequency arguments from the field rather than analytics. Navigation changed after six navigation variants had been produced with written pros and cons. A persistent menu had been recommended, but field reporting indicated that the menus were needed about once every two months and that almost nobody who used the panel needed them. The collapsed menu therefore won and was shown collapsed by default.

A disabled-station state was also deleted after both sites reported never having disabled one. The field evidence described one sensor replacement during the technician's tenure and spills occurring in corridors rather than on stations.

This engagement illustrates evidence-led prioritisation as the discipline of not building the design around rare exceptions while still deciding how those exceptions should be indicated.

bodySections.heading: Evidence-Led Prioritisation Can Support Staging and Disclosure Under Constraint
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Streetec kntrl 2 shows evidence-led prioritisation as staging. Testing produced a small set of immediate changes to screen transitions and a larger backlog of possible future features. Streetec chose to stage the larger backlog over a longer horizon rather than build it immediately.

Egma Order shows evidence-led prioritisation as disclosure under time pressure. When remaining time looked short during the UI phase, Creative Navy stated openly what would be completed first and what would be dropped if necessary rather than silently descoping.

The industrial engagement with a European industrial automation vendor shows mid-engagement re-prioritisation. The expert review was re-prioritised at the client's request because the client was already redesigning certain screens and wanted depth where the findings would still be actionable.

bodySections.heading: AIT, MDU and Assemblio Used Prioritisation to Reduce or Defer Work
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The AIT heat pump controller engagement made three decisions by reducing rather than adding. Widget content was cut to three pieces of information each on legibility grounds after AIT's own review of a wireframe at physical size raised concern about smaller text for an older installer. The commissioning flow was reordered so that mode and feature selection came before the commissioning assistant. The information feature was deferred with a defined interim behaviour because the needed content did not exist.

The MDU ship motion monitoring engagement made reductions by judgement. The live Now value was removed from both cards because it cost attention without adding information. Pinch-to-zoom was declined on implementation-cost grounds, with a tap-to-read-value interaction specified instead. Features such as remote viewing and settings change, hogging, sagging and twisting, parametric roll detection and warning, and heave, sway and surge were reserved for a defined place rather than partially implemented. Parametric roll detection and the alarm-versus-warning distinction were not built.

The Assemblio engagement staged out hyperlinks and step numbers on hover. It also recorded a harder prioritisation limit: the match list did not scale, a search field was identified as a clear improvement, and beyond that the documented discussion acknowledged that a better representation might not exist if the planner had to decide part by part.

bodySections.heading: Topera and Visioncheckout Prioritised Against External or Hardware Constraints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Topera was a concept design, and nothing was built. The prioritisation was set by interoperability depth rather than a feature list. Synchronisation levels were specified as required, target, stretch and post-MVP, and CPM collaboration classes were tiered in the same way. The concept design used the ProSTEP iViP and VDA recommendations as an external, published and verifiable yardstick. It also tiered data model coverage across the thirteen DIN 69901-4 diagrams. The concept design can be described as grounded in DIN 69901, but no compliance claim or outcome claim is established.

The visioncheckout engagement prioritised recommendations by constraint rather than preference. visioncheckout accepted every recommendation that did not require hardware change. Hardware-dependent recommendations, including the 3.5 mm headphone jack and tactile navigation keypad, were added to the requirements list for the next hardware iteration. This is not a claim that the product is accessible, will be accessible or complies with anything, and no shipped outcome is established.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries of Evidence-Led Prioritisation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Evidence-led prioritisation does not make weak evidence strong. It makes evidence strength visible so that a design team can decide whether to proceed, test further or defer.

The practice does not remove the need for further validation where evidence is observed but not quantified or inferred. In the confidence framework, inferred evidence is useful for generating hypotheses but not for high-stakes commitments without further testing.

The practice also depends on preserving evidence labels. Client-reported evidence should not be treated as measured evidence. Observed but not quantified evidence should not be treated as precise. Inferred evidence should not be treated as directly observed.

In the Maritime VTS example, counts must not be combined across stages. The 36 unique issues did not grow; later observations were mapped back into the same register. Combining register counts would create a false claim.

strongClaims: Evidence-led prioritisation ranks design options by combining expected operational effect with evidential confidence.
The evidential confidence framework distinguishes measured, client-reported, observed but not quantified and inferred evidence.
The practice produces a structured comparison document that supports parallel comparison, gap acknowledgement, disagreement resolution and decision audit.
Creative Navy uses evidence-led prioritisation during Concept Convergence, Implementation Partnership, audit work, product vision engagements and stakeholder alignment work.
IDEXX Animana used explicit prioritisation logic for more than 100 recommendations after a 35-clinic, 150-plus participant research programme.
Triopsis used evidence-led prioritisation after a 47-microtask analysis and recorded 62% faster job discovery and 83% faster job sequence optimisation.

The Maritime VTS engagement maintained an auditable register in which 36 unique issues were mapped to 28 traceable interaction requirements, 14 approved decisions, 18 rejected alternatives and a handover status register.
Raymarine applied four evidence classes to every decision in the register: comparative prototype evidence, scenario observation, design reasoning and technical dependency.
Topera was scoped as a concept design using interoperability depth and external recommendations, with no build and no outcome claim.

visioncheckout accepted recommendations that did not require hardware change and moved hardware-dependent recommendations to the next hardware iteration requirements list, with no shipped outcome or accessibility claim established.
limitations: Evidence-led prioritisation does not make weak evidence strong; it makes the confidence level visible.
Measured, client-reported, observed but not quantified and inferred evidence carry different confidence levels and should not be collapsed into a single evidence category.
Client-reported evidence depends on the client's measurement basis and objectivity.
Observed but not quantified evidence is directional rather than precise.
Inferred evidence is lowest confidence and is useful for hypotheses rather than high-stakes commitments without further validation.
The Maritime VTS counts must not be averaged or combined across register stages; the 36 unique issues did not grow, and later observations mapped back into the register.
In the Maritime VTS register, mitigated means addressed in design specifications and evaluated where in scope; it does not mean implemented, proven, certified or cleared from formal safety review.
AIT deferrals are design reasoning and client review evidence, not user-validated findings.
Topera was a concept design only; nothing was built and no outcome claim exists.
visioncheckout has no shipped outcome, accessibility claim or compliance claim in the available evidence.
Streetec staging should be framed as staging over a longer horizon, not reluctance.
